stem: She will succeed __________
optA: unless she works hard.
solution: First (open) conditional: a future result in the main clause takes a present-tense 'if' clause, so 'She will succeed if she works hard.' 'Unless' reverses the logic to a negative condition, 'even though' makes hard work a concession that should defeat success, and 'because' asserts the cause as an accomplished fact rather than the condition the stem sets up. Matches option C.

stem: He __________ to the party if he had been invited.
optA: would go
solution: Third conditional: 'if + had been invited' (past perfect) forces 'would have + past participle' in the main clause. 'Would go' belongs to the second conditional, 'had gone' repeats the if-clause form in the wrong slot, and the bare past 'went' cannot express an unreal past result. Matches option B.

stem: By the time we arrive, they __________
optA: will watch the movie.
solution: 'By the time' plus a present-tense clause about the future requires the future perfect for the action completed before that point: 'they will have watched the movie'. Simple future, present continuous and present perfect all fail to place the viewing before our arrival. Matches option C.

stem: I would have helped you if you __________
optA: ask me earlier.
solution: Third conditional again: the main clause 'I would have helped' fixes the if-clause as past perfect, 'if you had asked me earlier'. 'Ask' and 'asked' give the wrong tense for an unreal past, and 'would' is never used in the if-clause of a standard conditional. Matches option C.

stem: Neither the teacher nor the students __________
optA: is ready for the presentation.
optD: would been ready for the presentation.
solution: With 'neither ... nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, and the nearer subject here is the plural 'students', so 'are ready' is correct. 'Is' follows the distant singular 'teacher', option C omits the verb entirely, and 'would been' is not a possible verb form. Matches option B.

stem: Every one of the books ____
optA: have been returned to the library.
optB: were been returned to the library.
optC: are been returned to the library.
optD: has been returned to the library.
solution: The head of the subject is the singular 'Every one'; 'of the books' is only a prepositional phrase and cannot control the verb, so the singular 'has been returned' is required. 'Have been' agrees with the wrong noun, and 'were been' and 'are been' are impossible passive forms. Matches option D.

stem: Neither of the two candidates _____
optA: is qualified for the job.
solution: 'Neither' as a pronoun is singular and takes a singular verb, so 'Neither of the two candidates is qualified'. 'Are' and 'were' take plural agreement from the intervening 'candidates', and 'have qualified' both mis-agrees and changes the meaning from a state to a completed action. Matches option A.

stem: No sooner did the thieves see the police ___
optA: than they run away.
solution: 'No sooner ... than' is the fixed correlative, and after inversion in the past ('did the thieves see') the second clause must be simple past with a plural pronoun matching 'thieves': 'than they ran away'. A keeps the present 'run', B adds an ungrammatical 'start run', and C switches to the singular 'he'. Matches option D.

stem: We will miss the train ___
optA: until we start now
solution: 'Unless' means 'if not' and supplies the negative condition that averts the stated result: we will miss the train if we do not start now. 'Until' marks time rather than condition, 'if only' expresses a wish, and 'would we start' is an inversion with no trigger here. Matches option D.

stem: He avoided looking at her,___
optA: lest he think he was staring.
optB: lest she think he was staring.
optC: lest she thinking he was staring.
optD: lest she think he kept staring.
solution: 'Lest' takes the bare subjunctive, and the person who might form the impression is the woman he avoided looking at, so 'lest she think he was staring'. A puts the wrong subject with the verb, C replaces the subjunctive with a participle, and D shifts to 'kept staring', which contradicts a man who was avoiding her. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Option D is also grammatically well formed; it is rejected on sense only, since 'kept staring' contradicts the stem's 'avoided looking at her'.

stem: Had the witnesses not come forward,
optA: the accused would have been acquitted.
optB: the case is closed by now.
optD: the truth will never be known.
solution: 'Had the witnesses not come forward' is an inverted third conditional if-clause, so the main clause must be 'would have + past participle': 'the accused would have been acquitted'. B, C and D use present, past and future forms that cannot express an unreal past consequence. Matches option A.

stem: The director insisted that every team member
optA: attends the meeting regularly.
optD: should be attending the meeting regularly.
solution: 'Insist that' triggers the mandative subjunctive, so the verb stays in the bare form regardless of the singular subject: 'that every team member attend'. 'Attends' is the indicative, 'attending' has no finite verb, and the periphrastic 'should be attending' both adds a modal the subjunctive replaces and shifts to the continuous. Matches option C.

stem: Such was the intensity of the storm
optA: that even the strongest trees were uprooted.
solution: Inversion after fronted 'Such was ...' requires the correlative 'that' clause of result: 'Such was the intensity of the storm that even the strongest trees were uprooted.' 'So', 'which' and 'because' break the such-that pairing and give a coordination, a relative clause and a reason clause instead of the required result. Matches option A.

stem: If she were in your place,
optA: she would have accept the offer.
solution: Second conditional: the hypothetical past subjunctive 'If she were' pairs with 'would + bare infinitive', giving 'she would accept the offer'. A mixes 'would have' with a bare verb, B uses a past perfect that belongs to the third conditional, and D's 'will' treats an unreal situation as a real one. Matches option C.

stem: Being a former athlete,
optA: the race was easily won by her.
solution: The participial phrase 'Being a former athlete' must modify the subject of the main clause, and only 'she' can be the former athlete. In A the race is described as the athlete, in B the people, and in D the event, so all three dangle. Matches option C.

stem: Despite having all the required documents,
optA: his application was surprisingly rejected.
optB: but he was still denied entry.
optC: yet the visa officer asked more questions.
solution: 'Despite' already carries the concession, so the main clause must stand alone without a second contrast word: 'his application was surprisingly rejected'. B adds 'but', C adds 'yet' and D adds 'although', each doubling the concessive link and leaving the sentence without a proper main clause. Matches option A.

stem: The committee objected to
optA: he being appointed as the chairman.
optB: his being appointed as the chairman.
solution: 'Object to' is followed by a gerund, and the gerund's subject takes the possessive: 'objected to his being appointed'. A uses the nominative 'he' before a gerund, C uses an infinitive after 'to' that 'object to' does not license, and D adds a that-clause with an indicative verb after the preposition. Matches option B.

stem: Walking across the campus late at night,
optA: strange shadows were seen on the wall.
solution: The opening participial phrase 'Walking across the campus late at night' must attach to the subject of the main clause, and only 'I' can do the walking. Shadows, library lights and silence cannot walk, so A, B and D are dangling modifiers. Matches option C.

stem: After working for ten hours without a break,
optA: he collapsed on the couch.
solution: 'After working for ten hours' is a participial phrase whose implied subject must be the person working, so 'he collapsed on the couch' is the only fit. The report, the computer and the documents cannot be the ones who worked ten hours, leaving B, C and D dangling. Matches option A.

stem: Painted in bright red and gold,
optA: the designer loved the new look.
solution: The past-participle phrase 'Painted in bright red and gold' must modify the thing that was painted, which is the door. A makes the designer painted, C makes 'we' painted and D makes the people painted, so all three are misplaced modifiers. Matches option B.

stem: The teacher warned the students ____.
optA: that they must not to cheat in the exam.
optB: not to cheat in the examination.
optD: that do not cheat in the exam.
solution: Reported commands with "warn" take the pattern warn + object + not to + bare infinitive, so "warned the students not to cheat" is the only correct form. A doubles the modal and the infinitive ("must not to"), while C and D keep the direct-speech imperative "don't cheat" inside a reported clause. Matches option B.

stem: The match was cancelled ____.
optA: because of it was raining heavily.
optD: for the reason of heavy raining.
solution: "Because of" and "due to" must be followed by a noun phrase, and "the heavy rains" is a clean noun phrase. A puts a full clause after "because of", C turns the verb into the non-noun "the raining", and D is the unidiomatic "for the reason of". Matches option B.

stem: He speaks Hindi fluently ____.
optA: because he lived in India for five years.
optB: so he live in France since five years.
optC: because he was living in France since five years.
optD: because he has been live in France.
solution: A completed stretch of past residence takes the simple past with "for": "he lived in India for five years", and living in India is what explains fluent Hindi. B uses "so he live" with "since five years", C wrongly pairs a past continuous with "since five years", and D has the impossible "has been live". Matches option A.

stem: If he had studied more seriously, ____.
optA: he would passed the examination.
optB: he had passed the exam easily.
optC: he would have passed the examination.
solution: The third conditional requires had + past participle in the if-clause and would have + past participle in the main clause. A drops "have", B repeats the past perfect in the result clause, and D uses "should passed". Matches option C.

stem: I would rather stay home tonight ____.
optA: than going to that boring party.
optB: than to go to that boring party.
optC: than go to that boring party.
optD: instead of went to the boring party.
solution: "Would rather" takes a bare infinitive on both sides of "than", so "stay home ... than go" is parallel. A uses a gerund, B inserts "to", and D mixes "instead of" with a past tense verb. Matches option C.

stem: The Supreme Court on Monday extended its status quo ______
optA: until further orders.
solution: "Until" marks the end point of a state that continues from now, which is what extending a status quo means. "Before", "when" and "despite" do not express the duration of the extension and produce nonsense with "further orders". Matches option A.

stem: The researchers were surprised to discover that their experiment ____ such unexpected results.
optA: yields
solution: Sequence of tenses: the yielding of results happened before the past act of discovering, so the earlier event takes the past perfect "had yielded". A and D use present and future after a past main clause, which breaks the backshift. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Option B "yielded" is not strictly ungrammatical; the past perfect in C is the more precise and the intended answer, but a strict marker could accept B.

stem: If the researchers had analyzed the data more thoroughly, they ____
optA: would had discovered answers.
solution: Third conditional again: "If ... had analyzed" demands "would have discovered" in the result clause. A writes "would had", C gives the second-conditional "would discover", and D uses the real-future "will discover". Matches option B.

stem: Scarcely had the team won the championship ___
optA: immediately the celebrations began.
solution: The fixed correlative is "Scarcely had + subject + past participle ... when + clause". A, B and D all leave the inverted "Scarcely had" opening without its obligatory "when" partner. Matches option C.

stem: People who spend more time in deep discussion ___
optA: rather than small talk seem happily.
optB: rather than small talk look happily.
optC: rather than small talk seem to be happier.
optD: prior than small talk appear to be happier
solution: "Seem" and "look" are linking verbs and take an adjective, not the adverb "happily", and the comparison set up by "more time ... rather than" needs the comparative "happier". A and B use "happily", and D uses the non-existent "prior than". Matches option C.

stem: Never before
optA: the region experienced such devastation.
optB: had the region experienced such devastation.
optC: the region had experienced such devastation.
optD: did the region experienced such devastation.
solution: The negative adverbial "Never before" in front position forces subject-auxiliary inversion, giving "had the region experienced". A and C keep normal order, and D inverts but then adds a past form after "did". Matches option B.

stem: Not until the final chapter
optA: does the argument fully unfold.
solution: "Not until" fronted is a negative adverbial and triggers inversion of the operator: "does the argument fully unfold". B and D keep normal order, and C follows "did" with the inflected "unfolds" instead of a bare infinitive. Matches option A.

stem: Little attention
optA: was paid to the ethical implications.
optB: did pay to the ethical implications.
optC: had paid to the ethical implications.
optD: has paying to the ethical implications.
solution: Here "Little attention" is the subject of the sentence, not a fronted adverbial, so no inversion occurs and the passive "was paid to" is required. B and C invert or use an active verb with no agent, and D has the impossible "has paying". Matches option A.

stem: What distinguishes this theory from others
optA: are its empirical foundations.
solution: Pseudo-cleft agreement: in 'What ... + verb + complement' the verb may agree with a PLURAL predicate complement, and the complement here is 'its empirical foundations', so 'are' is used. Option (c) drops to a singular 'foundation' and shifts to the past, and (d) shifts to the present perfect, with nothing in the sentence licensing either tense. The competing prescriptive rule treats the 'What ...' clause as a singular subject and would give 'is' (option b); both are attested in standard usage, and this paper keys the plural-complement agreement. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Official LWS key A adopted over the derived B. Genuinely arguable; see solution.

stem: However compelling the evidence,
optA: doubts persisted among critics.
solution: "However + adjective + subject" is itself a concessive clause, so the main clause follows directly with a finite verb: "doubts persisted". B adds a redundant "but" after a concessive, C shifts to a past perfect with no earlier reference point, and D is a fragment with no finite verb. Matches option A.

stem: Preeti suggests
optA: that I ask to your advice
optB: that I had asked your advice
optC: that I can have asked your advice
solution: 'Suggest' + that-clause uses base verb (bare infinitive): 'suggests that I ask your advice'. Matches option D: that I ask your advice.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row 59babca9-a4c0-4f35-97fa-1fa940ec0e10; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: We saw
optA: the older of all monuments in the city
optB: the old of all monuments in the city
optC: the oldest monument in the city
optD: an oldest of all monuments in the city
solution: Superlative 'oldest' with definite article 'the' for comparison among many. Matches option C: the oldest monument in the city.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row 545b7344-9e0f-4c61-b43b-3b4bb0af2d4e; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: Since you have been touring all day
optA: you must be tired
optB: you ought to have been tired
solution: 'Must be' expresses strong logical deduction in the present. Matches option A: you must be tired.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row cbb6e7c6-e402-49ac-8d58-2719b2406b96; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: His condition is serious, but
optA: it should be worse
optD: it had been going to be worse
solution: 'Could be worse' is the standard idiom meaning the situation is not as bad as possible. Matches option C: it could be worse.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row 24c76174-a4fc-4436-9c73-4f56d3b23cd8; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: I hope the bus comes soon because
optA: we waited for half an hour
optB: we have been waiting for half an hour
optC: we waiting for half an hour
optD: we could have been waiting for half an hour
solution: Present perfect continuous for action started in the past, still ongoing. Matches option B: we have been waiting for half an hour.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row ba71f20e-2b41-4cb0-8fb3-a7e1d8c193e5; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: Someone
optA: has spilt juice on the sofa
optB: should have spilt juice on the sofa
optC: have spilt juice on the sofa
optD: would spilt juice on the sofa
solution: Present perfect 'has spilt' (3rd person singular) for recent action with present result. Matches option A: has spilt juice on the sofa.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row d058b53f-76eb-45d8-b0f7-f0e2608dda71; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: What would you do
optA: if you found your lost toy?
optB: if you will have found your lost toy?
optC: if you would found your lost toy?
optD: if you have find your lost toy?
solution: Second conditional: 'would + base verb … if + past simple' for hypothetical situations. Matches option A: if you found your lost toy?
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row 7ccc2e48-9611-4c9a-9336-4f58dc6ca37d; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: If I were you
optA: I shouldn't buy that dress
solution: Second conditional with subjunctive 'were': 'If I were you, I wouldn't…'. Matches option B: I wouldn't buy that dress.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row 5b4141d1-f825-44b4-880b-69a1fb252017; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: I wish
optA: I could help you
solution: 'Wish' + past modal 'could' expresses an unreal wish about the present. Matches option A: I could help you.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row 4b380d83-06d1-44e1-a7e1-a14df2f59917; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: The efforts of the security services have not been quite
optA: upto the incredibility
solution: Idiom 'up to the mark' = meeting the required standard. Matches option D: upto the mark.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row f948480e-a2a4-4d42-b655-b09f0a154b8a; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: Struggling to keep pace with technological advancements, ______.
optA: executives devised new strategies to adapt
optC: the industry remained stagnant despite efforts
optD: investors hesitated to back emerging startups
solution: The introductory participial phrase "Struggling to keep pace..." must attach to the subject that follows, and executives are people who can struggle and then devise strategies to adapt. B attaches the struggle to "revenues", which cannot struggle, and the soaring revenues contradict the modifier. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Options C and D also supply subjects capable of struggling, so the item turns on coherence rather than pure grammar; A is the tightest cause-and-effect match with "to adapt".

stem: After months of negotiations, the two companies finally saw ______
optA: towards progress
solution: The idiom for reaching agreement after negotiation is "see eye to eye". B is the truncated "the light at the end" without "of the tunnel" and means relief rather than agreement, while "towards progress" and "common foot" are not English idioms after "saw". Matches option D.

stem: The product launch was delayed not because of supply chain issues, but rather ______.
optA: to unexpected manufacturing defects
optB: because of concerns regarding product safety
optD: as if the demand forecast was misjudged
solution: The "not ... but rather" correlative demands parallel structures, so "not because of supply chain issues" must be balanced by "but rather because of concerns regarding product safety". A gives "to", C gives the ungrammatical "on account logistical", and D gives the clause connector "as if". Matches option B.

stem: Unlike his predecessor, the new prime minister ______.
optA: has been more involved in economic policies
optB: making policies that were vastly different
solution: The subject "the new prime minister" needs a finite verb, and the comparison signalled by "Unlike his predecessor" is carried by the comparative "more involved". B has only a participle and no finite verb, C wrongly makes an active verb passive ("is prioritised"), and D fails third-person agreement ("focus"). Matches option A.

stem: Exhausted from the long journey, ______.
optA: the hotel provided a warm meal and a comfortable bed
optB: the travelers collapsed onto their hotel beds immediately
optC: it was clear they needed some rest before the next day
optD: the exhaustion could be seen on their faces
solution: The opening participial phrase "Exhausted from the long journey" must modify the subject of the main clause, and only the travelers can be exhausted. A attaches the exhaustion to the hotel, C to the dummy "it", and D to "the exhaustion" itself, so all three dangle. Matches option B.

stem: I will not pay for the goods
optA: till he sends me the bill again
optB: until he sends me the bill again
optC: if he sends me the bill again
optD: unless he sends me the bill again
solution: Keyed (c) to match the official LWS answer key. Teacher's note: on the plain reading 'I will not pay for the goods if he sends me the bill again' inverts the intended sense, since receiving the bill is the condition for PAYING rather than for refusing, and the same question already in the bank keys 'unless he sends me the bill again'. Options (a) 'till' and (b) 'until' also read acceptably. Graded per the official key. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Official LWS key C adopted over the derived D on the teacher's explicit instruction. Keyed against standard grammar, so held PRIVATE (status flawed) and never flipped PUBLIC. Duplicates bank row 613bd0e0-da66-45c7-860a-34b39eed2f69, which keys D and is LEFT UNCHANGED.

stem: I did not buy it
optA: because I did not like the look of it
optB: as far as I did not like the look of it
optC: anyway I did not like the look of it
optD: if I did not like the look of it
solution: The sentence requires a causal conjunction; 'because' correctly gives the reason for not buying. Matches option A: because I did not like the look of it.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row 8a43f004-72d1-4713-b16d-b135fa42cdf3; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: I sent her a bouquet of orchids
optA: for which she was absolutely delighted
optB: with which she was absolutely delighted
optC: of which she was absolutely delighted
optD: on which she was absolutely delighted
solution: 'Delighted with' is the standard collocation; 'with which' is the correct preposition. Matches option B: with which she was absolutely delighted.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row 129893de-d35b-46a0-99ee-80f191747e79; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: You must stay inside
optA: where it starts raining
solution: The sentence requires a temporal subordinating conjunction; 'when' correctly indicates the time condition for staying inside. Matches option B: when it starts raining.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row d941bc3e-bc52-492e-a8af-8e39707316d4; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: We must wait
optA: until you see the light turn green
optB: till you see the green light
optC: because you can see the green light
optD: unless you see the red signal
solution: 'We must wait until you see the light turn green' sets the time boundary on the waiting. Option (c) inverts the sense, since a green light ends the wait rather than causing it, and (d) does the same with the red signal. Note that option (b) 'till you see the green light' says exactly the same thing as (a), because 'till' and 'until' are interchangeable, so the printed item has TWO correct options; (a) is keyed to match the official LWS key. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Official LWS key A adopted over the derived B. Printed item is DEFECTIVE: (a) and (b) are interchangeable, so two options are correct. Duplicate of bank row eddb22e6-b46c-4d51-af19-1a674d69c297; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: Which is the correct sentence?
optA: Although it was raining, we had the picnic.
optB: Although it was raining, still we had the picnic.
optC: Although it was raining, yet we had the picnic.
optD: Although it was raining, even then we had the picnic.
solution: 'Although' is a subordinating conjunction that does not need 'still', 'yet', or 'even then' as correlatives; the clause stands alone. Matches option A: Although it was raining, we had the picnic.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row 682d5acf-d079-4efb-a8f5-cc277c3463d1; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: Which is the correct sentence?
optA: When I would arrive, I will call you.
optB: When I shall arrive, I will call you.
optC: When I will arrive, I will call you.
optD: When I arrive, I will call you.
solution: In time clauses with 'when', simple present (not future tense) is used to refer to a future event. Matches option D: When I arrive, I will call you.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row 27ef0c9a-dceb-4a50-8cd5-139b60b033b6; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: Which is the correct sentence?
optA: Who among you has the answer?
optB: Whom among you has the answer?
optC: Whom amongst you has the answer?
optD: Who amid you has the answer?
solution: Keyed (c) to match the official LWS answer key. Teacher's note: 'whom' is the objective case and cannot serve as the subject of the verb 'has', so on standard grammar 'Who among you has the answer?' (option a) is the well-formed sentence. The same question already in the bank keys (a). Graded per the official key. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Official LWS key C adopted over the derived A on the teacher's explicit instruction. Keyed against standard grammar, so held PRIVATE (status flawed) and never flipped PUBLIC. Duplicates bank row 1a5d37b5-0028-4c5c-b06f-bc4ce84f0ad1, which keys A and is LEFT UNCHANGED.

stem: Which is the correct sentence?
optA: No sooner than he reached the station the train left.
optB: No sooner had he reached the station than the train left.
optC: No sooner he had reached the station than the train left.
optD: No sooner had he reached the station then the train left.
solution: 'No sooner...than' requires subject-auxiliary inversion after 'no sooner' and the correlative 'than' (not 'then'). Matches option B: No sooner had he reached the station than the train left.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row d1da041b-e9dc-47e3-b384-eef878a56251; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: Which is the correct sentence?
optA: Hardly had I arrived at the airport than the plane departed.
optB: Scarcely had I arrived at the airport when the plane departed.
optC: Hardly I had arrived at the airport when the plane departed.
optD: Scarcely had I arrived at the airport then the plane departed.
solution: 'Scarcely...when' (not 'than' or 'then') is the correct pair; inversion required after 'scarcely'. Matches option B: Scarcely had I arrived at the airport when the plane departed.
reviewNote: Duplicate of bank row 584930b3-04d3-4f0e-8690-fff489f0369d; answer + solution copied from it (printed option order identical).

stem: The little water that remained in the desert camp ______.
optA: were sufficient for everyone.
optD: was carefully rationed among the survivors.
solution: Rule: an uncountable noun ('water') takes a singular verb, and 'the little water that remained' is the singular head of the subject. Options A and B use the plural 'were' and C uses the plural 'have been', all of which disagree with the uncountable singular subject. Matches option D.

stem: A variety of rare medicinal plants grow naturally in this rainforest; however, ______.
optA: the variety found here are steadily decreasing.
optB: the variety found here is steadily decreasing.
solution: Rule: 'A variety of + plural noun' takes a plural verb, but 'The variety of' is itself the singular head and takes a singular verb, so 'the variety found here is' is correct. A uses the plural 'are' with the singular head 'variety'; C pairs 'every species' with the plural 'have'; D pairs 'each' with a plural noun and plural verb. Matches option B.

stem: Every member of the expedition carried emergency supplies; however, ______.
optA: each was responsible for using them wisely.
optB: each were responsible for using them wisely.
optC: every were responsible for using it wisely.
optD: all member was responsible for using it wisely.
solution: Rule: the distributive pronoun 'each' is singular and takes a singular verb. B pairs 'each' with the plural 'were'; C misuses 'every', which is a determiner and cannot stand alone as a pronoun; D pairs the plural 'all' with the singular noun 'member' and singular verb 'was'. Matches option A.

stem: Only after the encrypted files had been recovered ______.
optA: has the investigators identified the source of the cyberattack.
optB: the investigators identified the source of the cyberattack.
optC: did the investigators identify the source of the cyberattack.
optD: the investigators did identify the source of the cyberattack.
solution: Rule: when a sentence opens with the restrictive adverbial 'Only after ...', the main clause must invert with a dummy auxiliary, giving 'did + bare infinitive'. B and D keep normal subject-verb order, and A uses 'has' with the plural subject 'investigators' and also gives the wrong tense for a completed past sequence. Matches option C.

stem: The intelligence report was far from complete; ______.
optA: several crucial details had yet to be verified.
optD: however it was containing no errors.
solution: Rule: after a semicolon the second clause must be independent and must extend the idea logically; 'far from complete' is properly followed by details still awaiting verification. B contradicts the first clause and pairs 'every' with the plural 'conclusions were'; C misuses 'despite' before a finite clause; D uses the ungrammatical continuous 'was containing' and again contradicts the sense. Matches option A.

stem: During the Arctic expedition, the researchers discovered that the glacier had been retreating far more rapidly than anyone ______.
optA: has anticipated
solution: Rule: of two past events, the earlier one takes the past perfect; the anticipating happened before the past act of discovering, so 'had anticipated' is required. A ('has anticipated') is present perfect, C ('anticipates') is present simple, and D ('would anticipate') is a conditional form, none of which anchors the earlier past event. Matches option B.

stem: No sooner had the rescue helicopter landed than the medical team ______.
optA: rushed towards the injured climbers.
optB: had rushed towards the injured climbers.
optD: was rushing towards the injured climbers.
solution: Rule: the 'No sooner had + past participle ... than' pattern takes the simple past in the 'than' clause, since the past perfect already marks the earlier action. B repeats the past perfect, C shifts to the present simple, and D uses the past continuous, which does not convey the immediate completed response. Matches option A.

stem: The biologist objected to ______ into the protected nesting grounds without prior approval.
optA: tourists having enter
solution: Rule: 'object to' is followed by a gerund, and the doer of that gerund takes the possessive case, so the plural possessive 'tourists' entering' is required. A is an ungrammatical mix of participle and bare infinitive, B wrongly uses an infinitive after 'to', and C gives a bare singular possessive with no determiner, which does not fit the general plural sense. Matches option D.

stem: Rarely ______ such extraordinary northern lights visible so far south.
optA: people have seen
solution: Rule: a sentence beginning with the negative adverb 'Rarely' forces subject-auxiliary inversion, giving 'have people seen'. A and C keep normal word order, and D both fails to invert correctly and uses the ungrammatical 'had people seeing'. Matches option B.

stem: The hikers would have reached the summit before sunset, ______.
optA: unless the blizzard had delayed them not.
optB: if the blizzard would not delay them.
optC: if the blizzard had not delayed them.
solution: Rule: the third conditional pairs 'would have + past participle' in the main clause with 'if + past perfect' in the condition clause. A doubles the negative with 'unless ... not', B uses 'would' inside the if-clause, and D shifts to a present-tense open condition that clashes with 'would have reached'. Matches option C.

stem: The economist attributed the sudden fall in inflation not to reduced consumer demand but ______.
optA: to improved supply chains.
solution: Rule: the correlative 'not to X but to Y' demands parallel structure, so the preposition 'to' from 'attributed ... to reduced consumer demand' must be repeated. B omits 'to' entirely, and C and D substitute 'because of' and 'by', breaking both the parallelism and the fixed collocation 'attribute something to something'. Matches option A.

stem: There is no point ______ over decisions that cannot now be changed.
optA: worrying
solution: Rule: the fixed expression 'There is no point' is followed by a gerund, giving 'no point worrying'. B uses an infinitive, C uses a past participle with no auxiliary, and D is the ungrammatical 'having worry'. Matches option A.

stem: So convincing ______ that even experienced art historians initially believed it to be genuine.
optA: the forgery was
solution: Rule: when the complement 'So + adjective' is fronted, the subject and verb invert, giving 'So convincing was the forgery'. A and D keep normal subject-verb order, and C inverts but shifts to the present perfect, which clashes with the past-tense 'believed' in the result clause. Matches option B.

stem: ______ students from the Naval Academy have volunteered for the high-altitude survival camp, and all of them have already completed the preliminary medical examination.
optA: Every number of
solution: Rule: 'A number of + plural noun' takes a plural verb, and the sentence supplies 'have volunteered' and 'all of them'. B ('The number of') is singular and would require 'has', C ('The variety of') is likewise singular, and A ('Every number of') is not an English quantifier. Matches option D.

stem: Although Mathematics was his weakest subject in school, ______.
optA: he eventually became an accomplished data scientist.
optB: the equations were solved by great difficulty.
optC: the subject have never interested him afterwards.
solution: Rule: a clause opening with 'Although' sets up a contrast that the main clause must complete, and weakness at school contrasted with later success does exactly that. B is an unidiomatic passive ('solved by great difficulty' for 'with great difficulty') and offers no contrast, C pairs the singular 'the subject' with the plural 'have', and D pairs 'every theorem' with the plural 'confuse'. Matches option A.

stem: The Zojila tunnel will not be fully functional for civilian traffic
optA: till two years have passed.
solution: Rule: a negative main clause takes 'not ... until' to mark the point up to which the situation holds. B ('unless') states a condition rather than a time limit and produces a nonsensical reading, and D ('if') likewise turns a time boundary into a condition. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Printed item appears defective: option A ('till two years have passed') is a straightforward variant of option C ('until two years have passed') and is equally grammatical, so two options are effectively correct. Keyed to C because 'until' is the standard written form.

stem: The underground works for the tunnel were highly challenging
optA: because of the terrain was difficult.
optD: due to the terrain was difficult.
solution: Rule: 'because' is a subordinating conjunction and takes a full finite clause, whereas 'because of' and 'due to' are prepositional and take a noun phrase. A and D wrongly attach a finite clause to the prepositional forms, and C follows 'because' with a bare noun phrase and no verb. Matches option B.

stem: The workers had to deal with massive snow accumulation,
optA: for which they used a fleet of snow blowers.
optB: to which they used a fleet of snow blowers.
optC: at which they used a fleet of snow blowers.
optD: by which they used a fleet of snow blowers.
solution: Rule: the preposition in a 'preposition + which' relative clause must be the one the verb actually requires; one uses snow blowers 'for' a problem such as snow accumulation. 'Use ... to which', 'at which' and 'by which' are not the collocations governed by 'used', so B, C and D fail. Matches option A.

stem: Historically, travellers faced severe hardships in Ladakh
optA: where heavy snow closed the Zojila Pass for 4-6 months.
optB: when heavy snow closed the Zojila Pass for 4-6 months.
optC: unless heavy snow closed the Zojila Pass for 4-6 months.
optD: till heavy snow closed the Zojila Pass for 4-6 months.
solution: The opening adverbial 'Historically' sets a time frame, and the completion says WHEN the hardship was felt: travellers suffered when heavy snow closed the Zojila Pass for four to six months. Option (c) 'unless' inverts the condition and (d) 'till' makes the closure the end of the hardship rather than its occasion. Option (a) 'where' is also grammatical, taking the place noun 'Ladakh' as its antecedent, so the item turns on which reading is intended; the temporal one is keyed. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Official LWS key B adopted over the derived A. Genuinely arguable; see solution. Mildly ambiguous: option B ('when heavy snow closed the Zojila Pass') is also grammatical as a temporal clause. Keyed to A because the adjacent antecedent 'Ladakh' is a place, which the relative adverb 'where' picks up directly.

stem: The project is expected to spur long-term benefits in the region,
optA: although the breakthrough was achieved on June 9, 2026.
optB: in spite of the breakthrough was achieved on June 9, 2026.
optC: despite of the breakthrough being achieved on June 9, 2026.
optD: even though the breakthrough achieving on June 9, 2026.
solution: Rule: 'although' is a subordinating conjunction and takes a full finite clause, while 'in spite of' and 'despite' are prepositional and take a noun or gerund phrase. B attaches a finite clause to 'in spite of', C uses the non-existent 'despite of', and D leaves 'the breakthrough achieving' without a finite verb. Matches option A.

stem: Vinod is clearly ____ when it comes to speaking English.
optA: To a disadvantage
solution: Fixed prepositional idiom: one is 'at a disadvantage' (as with 'at an advantage', 'at ease', 'at risk'). 'To', 'in' and 'on' are not collocated with 'disadvantage' in this sense, so A, C and D are all non-idiomatic. Matches option B.

stem: Despite prepping for days, ______.
optA: she still botched the interview
optC: she decided to ghost the recruiter
solution: 'Despite' is a concessive connector, so the completion must CONTRAST with the preparation described in the first clause. Only A supplies a negative outcome despite the prepping; B and D are consistent outcomes (no contrast) and C is an unrelated action rather than a contrasting result. Matches option A.

stem: Although initial investigations pointed towards him_____.
optA: the preceding events corroborated his involvement in the crime
optB: the additional information confirmed his guilt
optC: the subsequent evidence that surfaced proved that he was innocent
optD: he gave an open confession of his involvement in the crime
solution: 'Although' signals concession, so the main clause must reverse the expectation set by 'initial investigations pointed towards him'. Only C reverses it (later evidence proved innocence); A, B and D all reinforce his guilt and therefore leave the concessive clause unexplained. Matches option C.

stem: Ever since he lost money in the stock market crash, he tends to ___.
optA: fight shy of any high-risk investments
optB: double down on the exact same volatile stocks.
optD: lose money in the stock market crash.
solution: 'Ever since he lost money...' demands a logical CONSEQUENCE of that loss, and 'tends to' requires a bare infinitive. A gives both: caution, expressed as 'fight shy of'. B is grammatical but is the opposite consequence, C uses a gerund after 'tends to' and is also illogical, and D merely repeats the cause as its own effect. Matches option A.

stem: Such was the complexity of the code ____ .
optA: that even the senior engineers were baffled.
optB: so the software release was delayed.
solution: The correlative structure 'Such was X that...' requires the clause of result to be introduced by 'that'. B ('so'), C ('which') and D ('because') all break the fixed 'such...that' pairing. Matches option A.

stem: If he were in your position,____ .
optA: he would have sign the contract.
solution: 'If he were' is the second (present unreal) conditional, whose main clause takes 'would' plus a bare infinitive. A is malformed ('would have sign'), B uses a past perfect main clause, and D uses 'will', which belongs to the first conditional. Matches option C.

stem: Being an experienced chef, _____ .
optA: the dish was flawlessly prepared by him.
optC: he prepared the gourmet meal effortlessly.
solution: The participial phrase 'Being an experienced chef' must modify the subject of the main clause, so that subject has to be the chef himself. Only C supplies 'he'; A ('the dish'), B ('critics') and D ('the restaurant') all leave the participle dangling. Matches option C.

stem: The board objected to ____ .
optA: he being promoted to the director.
optB: his being promoted to the director.
solution: 'Object to' is followed by a gerund, and the doer of that gerund is expressed by a possessive: 'his being promoted'. A uses the nominative 'he', C wrongly uses an infinitive after 'to', and D uses a finite that-clause, which 'object to' does not take here. Matches option B.

stem: Driving through the mountain pass late at night, _____ .
optA: thick fog was encountered on the road.
optC: I saw a deer crossing the road.
solution: The introductory participial phrase 'Driving through the mountain pass' must attach to the subject of the main clause, which must therefore be the person driving. Only C gives a human agent, 'I'; A, B and D make fog, headlights and darkness the driver, leaving the modifier dangling. Matches option C.

stem: After rendering a high-resolution 3D video for ten hours, ____ .
optA: the laptop overheated and shut down.
solution: 'After rendering... for ten hours' is a participial phrase whose implied subject must be the thing that did the rendering, and it must be followed by a consequence of that ten-hour load. A supplies the laptop as agent and overheating as the consequence; B and D are passive clauses whose subjects ('the project', 'the files') did no rendering, and C both misassigns the agent and states an illogical result. Matches option A.

stem: What sets this brand apart from its competitors __________.
optA: are its innovative marketing strategies.
optD: have been its innovative marketing strategies.
solution: Pseudo-cleft agreement, identical in form to Q34: the verb agrees with the plural predicate complement 'its innovative marketing strategies', giving 'are'. Option (c) shifts to the past with a singular 'strategy' and (d) to the present perfect, neither licensed by the sentence. The competing prescriptive rule would treat 'What sets this brand apart' as a singular subject and give 'is' (option b); both are attested, and this paper keys the plural-complement agreement consistently across both twins. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Official LWS key A adopted over the derived B. Genuinely arguable; see solution.

stem: The instructor warned the divers ____.
optA: that they must not to panic underwater.
solution: 'Warn' takes the pattern 'warn someone not to do something', that is, object plus 'not to' plus bare infinitive. A mixes the that-clause with an infinitive ('must not to panic'), and C and D wrongly retain the imperative form inside reported speech. Matches option B.

stem: The festival was postponed ____.
optA: because of it was snowing heavily.
optD: for the reason of heavy snowing.
solution: 'Due to' and 'because of' are followed by a NOUN PHRASE, so 'due to the heavy snowfall' is correct. A puts a finite clause after 'because of', C forces the verb 'snowing' to act as a noun, and D is a wordy non-idiomatic construction. Matches option B.

stem: She codes in Python fluently ____.
optA: because she worked at a tech firm for five years.
optB: so she work in Munich since five years.
optC: because she was working in Munich since five years.
optD: because she has been work in Munich.
solution: Only A is well formed: 'because' introduces a finite clause and the past simple takes 'for five years' to measure duration. B has a subject-verb agreement error ('she work') plus the wrong preposition, C uses 'since' with a period of time instead of a point in time, and D leaves the participle out of the present perfect continuous ('has been work'). Matches option A.

stem: I would rather order takeout tonight ____.
optA: than going to that crowded restaurant.
optB: than to go to that crowded restaurant.
optC: than go to that crowded restaurant.
optD: instead of went to the crowded restaurant.
solution: 'Would rather' takes a bare infinitive in both halves of the comparison: 'would rather order... than go'. A uses a gerund, B inserts 'to', and D replaces the required 'than' with 'instead of' and adds a past tense. Matches option C.

stem: The proposal appeared convincing at first sight; however, ________.
optA: its implementation received unanimous administrative support.
optB: its underlying assumptions failed under closer scrutiny.
optC: its recommendations were circulated among all departments.
optD: its authors defended it with considerable enthusiasm.
solution: 'However' is an adversative connector, so the second clause must contradict the favourable first impression stated before the semicolon. Only B does so, opposing 'convincing at first sight' with failure 'under closer scrutiny'; A, C and D are all neutral or positive continuations that give the contrast nothing to work against. Matches option B.

stem: Although the expedition ultimately failed to achieve its principal objective, ________.
optA: it yielded observations of considerable scientific importance.
optB: the weather remained favourable throughout the journey.
optC: the organisers had anticipated every possible contingency.
optD: its members displayed poor physical endurance.
solution: 'Although' is concessive: the main clause must offer a positive counterweight to the expedition's failure. A does this by crediting it with valuable observations, whereas B and C are unrelated background facts and D compounds the failure instead of contrasting with it. Matches option A.

stem: The witness answered every question without hesitation; nevertheless, ________.
optA: the audience remained attentive throughout the examination.
optB: the proceedings concluded considerably earlier than anticipated.
optC: the investigating officer expressed appreciation for his cooperation.
optD: the consistency of his testimony continued to invite careful scrutiny.
solution: 'Nevertheless' demands a clause that runs counter to the favourable impression created by answering 'without hesitation'. Only D withholds that credit by keeping the testimony under scrutiny; A and B are neutral observations and C actually reinforces the first clause rather than opposing it. Matches option D.

stem: Were it not for his timely intervention, the negotiations ________.
optA: will have collapsed
solution: 'Were it not for' is the inverted unreal conditional with 'if' omitted, and because the intervention is a completed past event the result clause takes the past-unreal form 'would have collapsed'. A wrongly uses the future perfect, B gives a present or future result that clashes with the past intervention, and D is a bare past perfect with no modal. Matches option C.
reviewNote: On a strictly present-time reading of 'Were it not for', option B ('would collapse') is also defensible; C is preferred here because 'his timely intervention' fixes the situation in past time, which is the standard key for this item.

stem: The chairman insisted that the meeting should continue, ________.
optA: until every objection had been considered.
optB: until every objection has been considered.
solution: After the past-tense main verb 'insisted', the sequence of tenses requires a past form in the subordinate clause, and the passive perfect 'had been considered' marks the objections as dealt with before the meeting could end. B keeps the present perfect after a past verb, C uses the active continuous where a passive is needed, and D fails both agreement and voice. Matches option A.
